item.title: Okayama Events 2026: Saidaiji Naked Festival, Momotaro & Korakuen
item.description: Okayama — the sunny “Land of Sunshine” on the Seto Inland Sea — mixes one of Japan’s wildest winter rituals with the serene beauty of a great garden. In February, thousands of men in loincloths battle for lucky sticks in near-darkness at Saidaiji; in summer, a festival named for the folk hero Momotaro fills the city with dance and fireworks; and year-round, the celebrated Korakuen garden glows with seasonal illuminations. This guide gathers the events worth planning a 2026 trip around, with a month-by-month calendar at the end.

item.title: Kibi Plain Cycling Route: Shrines, Kofun and Rice Fields — Guide
item.description: The Kibi Plain west of Okayama city was the heart of the ancient Kibi kingdom, and a dedicated cycling path now runs roughly 15 flat kilometres across it between Bizen-Ichinomiya and Soja stations. It is a near-perfect half-day ride: the route threads through rice paddies and villages past Kibitsuhiko Shrine, the National Treasure Kibitsu Shrine with its 400-metre corridor, a huge keyhole-shaped burial mound, the ruins of an ancient temple and a striking five-storey pagoda standing alone in the fields.

item.title: Kibidango: Momotaro's Millet Dumplings — Guide
item.description: Kibidango are small, soft, faintly sweet mochi dumplings dusted in powder, and in Okayama they carry a story: in the tale of Momotaro, the Peach Boy, it is kibidango that the hero gives to a dog, a monkey and a pheasant to win them as companions on his journey to defeat the demons. Since the Kibi Plain west of Okayama is widely held to be the origin of that legend, the dumplings have become the prefecture’s defining souvenir.

item.title: Kibitsu Shrine: The 400-Metre Corridor and the Momotaro Legend — Guide
item.description: Kibitsu Shrine, on the Kibi Plain west of Okayama city, is one of the most distinctive shrines in western Japan. Its main hall, rebuilt in 1425 and designated a National Treasure, has a rare twin-gabled roof form found nowhere else, called kibitsu-zukuri. From it, a covered wooden corridor runs some 400 metres along the contour of the hillside, rising and falling through the trees in a receding perspective that is unforgettable.

item.title: Okayama with Kids: Momotaro Shrines, Castle Views & Bizen Pottery
item.description: Okayama has an unusual advantage as a family destination: it is the birthplace of Momotaro, the Peach Boy who is arguably the most famous character in Japanese folklore. Every child in Japan grows up with the story of the boy born from a giant peach who recruits a dog, a monkey, and a pheasant as companions and goes to defeat the demons of Onigashima Island. In Okayama, this is not merely a story.
